opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to frame it is that team-wide memory is effectively shared infrastructure, so you want to treat changes to it a lot like you'd treat changes to a codebase. When an agent learns something in one person's session and that gets promoted into memory that everyone's agents read from, you've just changed the behavior of every downstream interaction. That's powerful, but it's also a surface for drift, for mistakes compounding, and frankly for someone slipping in instructions they shouldn't.

So a few principles we've landed on. First, separate proposing from committing. Agents can suggest a memory update, but the write to the shared layer should go through some review step, whether that's a human owner or at minimum a diff that people can see. Second, make memories small and attributable. One fact per entry, with where it came from and why it was added, so when something goes wrong you can trace it back and revert it cleanly rather than untangling a giant blob of context. Third, scope matters. A lot of what an agent learns is really personal preference or specific to one project, and it shouldn't be promoted to team-wide at all. The bar for "everyone's agent should believe this" ought to be higher than "this was useful once."

And then the last piece is that memory goes stale. Something that was true about the codebase three months ago might be wrong now, so you want the system to verify before acting on a recalled fact, and you want periodic pruning. Honestly, deleting memories is as important as adding them. The failure mode I worry about isn't the agent forgetting things, it's the agent confidently remembering things that are no longer true.

r001.rationale: It compares shared memory changes to codebase changes and proposes separating proposals from commits, with a review step or visible diff—an equivalent to pull-request-like review.

r002.rationale: It suggests review by a human owner, but does not say the reviewer deeply understands the affected system.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that team-wide memory should be reviewed the way you'd review a change to shared infrastructure, not the way you'd review a chat message. And most teams haven't internalized that yet.

Here's the way I think about it. When an agent learns something about one engineer's preferences, that's low stakes. Worst case, it's wrong for one person and they correct it. But when you write something into memory that every agent on the team is going to read before it acts, you've basically changed the behavior of the whole system. That's a config change. That's a deploy. So it should look like one.

Concretely, a few things matter. First, it should go through something like a pull request. Someone proposes "our deploy process is X" or "we always use this library for Y," and a human who actually owns that area signs off. Not just whoever happened to be talking to the agent that day. Second, it needs provenance. Where did this fact come from? Was it a decision the team made in a meeting, or was it one person's offhand comment that the agent generalized? Those are very different levels of trust, and the memory should carry that metadata with it. Third, you want it to be versioned and reversible, because memory rots. The thing that was true about your codebase six months ago may be actively harmful advice now, and if you can't see when it was written and roll it back, you're going to spend a lot of time debugging agents that are confidently doing the wrong thing for reasons nobody can trace.

The part people underestimate is the attack surface. If an agent can write to shared memory based on what it reads, then anything that can get text in front of that agent can potentially poison the whole team. A malicious comment in a dependency, a weird issue on GitHub. So I'd argue the write path to team memory should be gated harder than the read path, and probably shouldn't be fully autonomous at all in the near term.

The analogy I keep coming back to is: we spent twenty years building good hygiene around code review. Memory is going to need the same thing, and it's going to feel like overkill right up until it doesn't.

r001.rationale: It says team-wide memory changes should go through something like a pull request.

r002.rationale: It says a human who owns the affected area should sign off, identifying an area owner as the reviewer.

astra-6.text:
I’d treat changes to team-wide memory as changes to shared infrastructure. An agent can propose an update, but you want to see what changed, what evidence supports it, and who it affects before it becomes something everyone relies on.

The review should scale with the consequences. Fixing a stale link can be lightweight. Changing a team’s priorities or recording a decision as settled needs approval from someone responsible for that decision. And you want provenance and version history, so you can understand where a belief came from and roll it back. Otherwise, one mistaken inference can become the premise for everybody else’s work.

r001.rationale: It proposes that an agent submit an update for review, with the change, supporting evidence, and affected people examined before adoption—a pull-request-like process.

r002.rationale: It calls for approval by someone responsible for a decision when consequences are significant, but does not say the reviewer should deeply understand the affected system.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want to treat changes to team-wide memory a lot like changes to a shared codebase. An agent can propose an update, but it shouldn’t automatically become something that every other agent treats as true. You want to see what changed, where the information came from, and whether it conflicts with something you already know.

The level of review should depend on the consequence. Updating a routine project detail can be lightweight. Changing a shared objective or a constraint should require explicit approval. And you need versioning and rollback, because a bad memory can propagate across the entire team.

r001.rationale: It compares memory changes to changes in a shared codebase and says an agent can propose an update for review before it becomes shared truth, which communicates a pull-request-like process.

r002.rationale: It calls for review and explicit approval for consequential changes, but does not say the reviewer should deeply understand the affected system.
